transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-11-24
- Time: 15:00 PST
- Duration: ~47 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Dr. Anya Patel (CISO), Marcus Lee (Head of DevOps), Sofia Ramos (Legal), Evan Chu (Platform)

Auto sections (auto-summary may be imperfect)
Summary: security intake, deployment options, KMS and log retention talk
Topics: SOC2, SSO, RBAC, audit logs, encryption, data residency

Transcript body:
00:00 Speaker 1: Okay, um, thanks everyone for making time. This is Jordan from Redwood, I'm joined by Priya. We we appreciate you all jumping on.
00:08 Dr. Anya Patel: Thanks, Jordan. We'll go quick. I'm Anya, CISO for Monterey Biosystems. Big reason for this call is we need to evaluate options for inference hosting for a confidential research product.
00:18 Jordan (Redwood): Yep totally understood. Can you talk briefly about your compliance posture and must-haves so we can map Hosted/Dedicated/Private?
00:26 Dr. Anya Patel: Sure. We're SOC2 Type II in progress, target completion Q1. We also have ISO 27001 controls already in place for our core platform. For the inference part — must haves are: customer managed KMS or HSM, ability to keep data in our VPC, long audit log retention (2 years), SSO via SAML + SCIM provisioning, and RBAC down to project level. Also legal wants documented data retention and delete workflows, and proof of encryption at rest in all modes.
00:52 Priya (Redwood): That's helpful. Quick framing — our Hosted product gives the fastest onboarding but we understand it doesn't meet customer-managed KMS requirements. Dedicated gives reserved capacity and better isolation; Private (VPC/on-prem) is where we enable your KMS and full network control.
01:07 Marcus Lee: For us the biggest blocker to Hosted is KMS and VPC peering. We can't send sensitive PII to a multi-tenant key unless it's our key.
01:16 Jordan (Redwood): Totally makes sense. For Dedicated we do offer bring-your-own-key via cloud KMS integrations in some configs, but the strongest guarantee is Private where you can use your KMS and subnet. Priya, can you walk through the KMS flow we typically show?
01:28 Priya (Redwood): Sure. High-level — in Private/VPC we run a customer-facing control plane inside your environment or with an encrypted control channel. Model artifacts can be pulled into your network, the runtime attaches to your KMS for envelope keys. The model KV cache is encrypted with a data key which itself is protected by your KMS. There's an audit chain for crypto ops. I will share the diagram after. (slight pause) Note: in Dedicated we can do BYOK via cloud provider KMS but not full HSM-backed attestation without Private.
02:02 Evan Chu: Quick clarifying Q — when you say "pull model artifacts into our network" is that an S3 copy in our account or a sidecar? We have strict egress rules.
02:10 Priya (Redwood): Typically it's a one-time artifact pull into your S3 bucket (in Private), no outbound inference requests leave your VPC. For Dedicated it depends on the contract, sometimes it's a managed account setup with peered subnets. We'll include exact patterns.
02:23 Dr. Anya Patel: Audit logs — we need immutable logs of inference requests (metadata at minimum) with 2-year retention and exportable to our SIEM. Can Redwood support that?
02:34 Jordan (Redwood): Yes. We have an audit logging pipeline that can forward to customer syslog/Splunk/Datadog. For Hosted we retain logs for a default window but for enterprise we can route and retain per your SLA. Priya, any caveats?
02:44 Priya (Redwood): Caveat: payload-level retention is sensitive. We can mask or redact request bodies before they land in centralized logs, or we can keep raw logs inside your VPC if using Private. Export formats include JSONL with signed timestamps. We'll add immutable write-once option via S3 with bucket lock for retention policy.
03:06 Marcus Lee: What about tokenization? Our workloads send identifiable sequences. Do you support client-side tokenization or partial redaction?
03:13 Priya (Redwood): We recommend client-side PII tokenization as best practice for Hosted/Dedicated. For Private we can run a preprocess step in your VPC — either a Redwood preprocessor container under your control or you deploy your own tokenization lambda. Technical notes will be in the doc.
03:28 Sofia Ramos: Legal question — we need to know subprocessors and data flow. Who has access to raw request data in Dedicated vs Private?
03:36 Jordan (Redwood): In Dedicated, Redwood manages the runtime nodes but we offer strict role-based access for our ops team and can do contractually limited access. In Private, control plane ops access can be limited and can be run by your ops team — which reduces Redwood operator access to near zero depending on config. We'll provide a subprocessors list.
03:54 Speaker 2: (muffled) also will you provide SOC2 artifacts right now?
04:00 Jordan (Redwood): Yes — we can share the SOC2 Type II report and our security whitepaper. We'll sanitize any customer-identifying info as needed.
04:07 Dr. Anya Patel: Is Redwood itself SOC2? That's critical.
04:10 Jordan (Redwood): Yes, Redwood is SOC2 Type II certified; we'll send the report. We're also working on ISO documentation.
04:17 Evan Chu: Regarding RBAC: we need RBAC at the project level with service accounts, ability to scoping tokens to models and routes, and audit of token usage. Is that supported?
04:27 Priya (Redwood): Yes. Our token model supports scoped API keys, route-level permissions, and token expiry. For Private, you can integrate with your SSO and map groups to roles via SCIM and SAML attribute mapping. We also emit token usage logs to the audit pipeline.
04:44 Marcus Lee: How about session caching and KV cache — any risk that one customer session leaks to another in Dedicated?
04:51 Priya (Redwood): Not in standard configs; runtime isolates KV caches per tenant. We shard caches and enforce memory isolation. For extra assurance we can enable periodic cache eviction windows and attestations in Dedicated contracts.
05:06 Dr. Anya Patel: Data residency — our research datasets must remain in our AWS account US-West-2. Hosted options that store tokens outside that region are a no-go.
05:16 Jordan (Redwood): Understood. Private is straightforward for region lock; Dedicated can be region pinned depending on availability. Hosted generally has multi-region distribution unless you sign an enterprise contract for regional-only hosting. We'll mark regional constraints in the proposal.
05:30 Sofia Ramos: On retention and deletion — we need documented proof of deletion (evidence) when requested by a subject or internal audit. Is there a mechanism to purge request-level data across caches and backups?
05:42 Priya (Redwood): We implement a deletion workflow that traces through object storage, caches, and analytics pipelines. For Private, you get direct access to the deletion runbook and can trigger programmatic purges. For Hosted/Dedicated we provide an API and audit trail of deletion events; backups are covered via retention/expiry policies. There are edge cases with aggregated telemetry but those can be configured to exclude PII.
06:05 Marcus Lee: Performance SLA question — if we run Dedicated, what's the qps and p99 latency guarantees and does that impact the security posture?
06:13 Jordan (Redwood): Dedicated comes with committed throughput and latency SLOs depending on instance type. That doesn't change encryption controls. If you need both high throughput and your own KMS, Dedicated or Private is the route. We can run a benchmark with your payloads.
06:26 Evan Chu: For the benchmark, we need to see the memory/kv cache footprint and how batching influences tokenization — can Redwood provide a sample harness?
06:34 Priya (Redwood): Yes — we have a benchmarking harness. We'll share a script and doc. For Private we can run it inside your account to remove network variance.
06:42 Dr. Anya Patel: A few curveballs from legal — cross-border access. Some of our researchers are in EMEA. We need proof that keys and data do not leave jurisdiction.
06:52 Jordan (Redwood): With Private, keys stay in your KMS in the region. With Dedicated we can region-pin and restrict operator access to specific data centers; Hosted is more complicated. We'll include region-flow diagrams.
07:05 Sofia Ramos: We will also need to run Redwood's security questionnaire and vendor risk assessment. How long does it take to fill?
07:12 Jordan (Redwood): Our standard turnaround is 3–5 business days for the vendor questionnaire, faster if it's a templated shared doc. Priya will help with technical answers.
07:20 Sofia Ramos: Good. Also, indemnities and data processing addendum — any standard DPAs?
07:25 Jordan (Redwood): Yes, we have a standard DPA and can include custom clauses for enterprise. We'll pre-share a redlineable DPA with the SOC2/ISO packet.
07:33 Marcus Lee: A minor question — do you support customer-managed certificate rotation and HSM-backed signing for model images?
07:40 Priya (Redwood): For Private, yes. For Dedicated, we can integrate with customer KMS and do signed images; HSM-backed attestation requires Private/on-prem.
07:50 Evan Chu: On SSO: we use Okta + SAML, and have SCIM provisioning. What's the SCIM user sync cadence and group mapping?
07:58 Priya (Redwood): SCIM sync is near realtime with delta syncs; group mapping allows mapping Okta groups to Redwood roles. We'll share the exact attribute mappings and a sample SAML metadata file.
08:10 Dr. Anya Patel: One more compliance point: we run annual penetration tests and internal audits. Will Redwood provide test windows and coordinate with our testers?
08:19 Jordan (Redwood): Yes — we have a scheduled pentest window and an approved list of scanning rules. For Private, you can run your own tests; Dedicated/policies can be coordinated under contract.
08:30 (crosstalk)
08:34 Jordan (Redwood): Okay, to summarize immediate asks: SOC2 report, Private architecture diagram, KMS flow, audit log export patterns, SCIM/SAML metadata, vendor questionnaire. Anything else?
08:46 Sofia Ramos: Please include a data flow diagram that shows every Redwood subprocessor and operator role ID in the chain.
08:53 Jordan (Redwood): We'll include subprocessors and operator role descriptions.
08:57 Dr. Anya Patel: And price expectations for Dedicated vs Private; a ballpark to help procurement.
09:03 Jordan (Redwood): We'll put ballpark monthly for Dedicated + a separate Private onboarding cost. We'll avoid hard quotes until we see your throughput numbers.
09:10 Evan Chu: Let's schedule the benchmark after we share sample payloads.
09:14 Jordan (Redwood): Great. Priya — anything else technical to note?
09:17 Priya (Redwood): One note — for deletion proofs, we can provide signed manifests showing object-level purge times; for stronger guarantees we support bucket lock with legal holds managed by the customer.
09:28 Marcus Lee: That should work.
09:30 Jordan (Redwood): Thanks all — we'll follow up with the packet and a proposed schedule for the benchmark. We'll target Slack/email follow-ups.
09:38 Dr. Anya Patel: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript. Notes: occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., ISO12001 as noted in the next steps), speaker labels are auto-assigned and may not always map to exact voices.
